IB 2027 · HL · Unit 6

Unit 6: Abstract Data Types

HL curriculum overview and structured learning plan.

Introduction

How do we organize data when we don't know how much there is?

This unit focuses on Dynamic Structures. Unlike Arrays (which are fixed), ADTs like Linked Lists and Trees grow and shrink as needed. You will learn how to build these structures from scratch using nodes and pointers, and explore how Hashing allows for instant data retrieval.

You'll start by building dynamic chains (Linked Lists). Then you'll branch out into non-linear data (Binary Search Trees) and recursive traversals. Finally, you'll optimize search speed using Hash Tables.

Linked Lists

A chain of nodes, connected by pointers. Easy to grow, hard to search.

  • Singly Linked: Each node points to the Next one (Forward only).
  • Doubly Linked: Nodes point to Next and Previous (Bi-directional).
  • Circular: The Tail points back to the Head (No end).
Binary Search Trees (BST)

Organizing data hierarchically for faster searching.

  • Rules: Left child < Parent < Right child.
  • Benefit: Cuts search space in half at every step (O(log n)).
  • Structure: Defined recursively (A tree is a node with two sub-trees).
Tree Traversals

How do we visit every node in a tree?

  • In-Order: Left -> Root -> Right (Gives sorted output).
  • Pre-Order: Root -> Left -> Right (Good for copying trees).
  • Post-Order: Left -> Right -> Root (Good for deleting trees).
Hashing

Finding data instantly (O(1)).

  • Hash Function: Converts a Key (e.g., "Bob") into an Index (e.g., 5).
  • Collision: When two keys hash to the same index. We must handle this (e.g., by chaining).
Key Terminology
TermDefinition
ADT (Abstract Data Type) A logical description of how data is viewed and the operations that can be performed on it (Interface), separate from implementation.
Node The basic unit of a data structure, containing data and one or more pointers.
Pointer A reference to a memory location where the next node is stored.
Root The top node of a tree structure.
Leaf A node in a tree that has no children.
Hash Function An algorithm that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values (indexes).
Collision When a hash function assigns the same index to two different keys.
Traversal The process of visiting (checking/updating) each node in a tree data structure.

Applications

  • File Systems (Trees)
  • Dictionary Lookups (Hash Tables)
  • Route Finding (Graphs/Trees)
  • Compiler Syntax Analysis (Trees)
